newsitem.title: UK: SOCCER-ENGLAND AND GERMANY UNLIKELY TO CO-HOST 2006 WORLD CUP.
newsitem.headline: SOCCER-ENGLAND AND GERMANY UNLIKELY TO CO-HOST 2006 WORLD CUP.

text.p: England and Germany are unlikely to co-host the World Cup in 2006, Alec McGivan, the director of England's World Cup campaign, said on Tuesday.
"It has been mentioned to us a number of times but frankly I don't think it is an option," he said.
"I'm sure that if the bids from England and Germany were so strong that no one could choose between them, then it might be a possibilty.
"But so much would have to happen before that ever became an eventuality. I can't see it materialising."
McGivan was speaking the day before England's bid to host the finals in nine years was to be officially launched by British Prime Minister John Major.
His remarks followed developments last week which he admitted "seriously disrupted our strategic thinking on the bid".
Those developments began when UEFA, European soccer's ruling body, sent a surprise fax to the English Football Association saying UEFA would be supporting only Germany's bid to stage the finals.

Intense lobbying followed with UEFA general secretary Gerhard Aigner meeting English F.A. officials in London last Friday to say that UEFA would be considering bids by both England and Germany after all.

Bidding nations must submit their documents to FIFA, world soccer's governing body, by September 1999, with FIFA's 24-man executive committee deciding which country will stage the 2006 World Cup in June 2000.
"McGivan said: "During our bidding process we are not going to play down or be negative about any other nation's bid. We are going to emphasise what England has to offer.

"There are six good reasons why England should stage the World Cup -- It is the birthplace of the game; Euro 96 was an outstanding success; England's grounds are now the finest in the world; The rebuilt Wembley Stadium will perhaps be the finest football stadium in the world; there is a unique atmosphere at games in England and England is a great place to visit."

The English F.A., backed by both the Conservative government and Labour opposition, are budgeting between eight and 10 million pounds sterling ($12.8 and 16 million) over the next three years in their efforts to bring the World Cup to England for the first time since 1966.
